## Overview

This analysis produces **national estimates of plant species' trait means** for
Australia, as part of the ARDC-funded AusTraits programme. Trait data are sampled
unevenly across each species' geographic and climatic range, so a simple average
is biased toward wherever a species happened to be measured. Instead, for each
trait we estimate the species-level mean **at the centre of the species' climate
distribution** (the 2D precipitation–temperature medoid), giving a consistent,
defensible reference point across species and traits.

We use a hierarchical within-group-centred model. Predictors are centred on the
medoid (`x_c = obs − medoid`), so the between-species terms describe turnover
across the continent and the within-species terms describe how a trait shifts
across a species' range. This serves two goals: (1) delivering the species-mean
estimates for AusTraits, and (2) underpinning a paper that reports these means
and gives credence to the estimates (uncertainty intervals, the within/between
decomposition, and — via the BRMS backend — full posterior inference). See
`demo.qmd` for the statistical motivation and `refactor_plan.md` for the design.

This notebook is a *reporting layer*: model fitting, exports and figures are
produced by the `targets` pipeline (`_targets.R`); here we `tar_load()` the
results and narrate them. The dataset (`dataset_construction.qmd`) combines plant
height from AVH with the remaining traits from AusTraits. Two interchangeable
fitting backends are available — `tmb` (fast, used here) and `brms` (full
posterior, opt-in via `run_brms` in `_targets.R`) — behind one interface
(`fit_trait_climate_model()`); all logic lives in `R/`.

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(targets)
source("R/init.R")

tar_load(trait_summary)   # fitted fixed effects per trait
tar_load(tmb_fits)        # list of per-trait fits (with $centres)
tar_load(combined)        # integrated best-estimate product
tmb_fits <- purrr::compact(tmb_fits)
out_dir <- "outputs/traits"
```

## Fit per-trait models

One model per trait (TMB), keeping species with more than `n_min` records. Each
fit yields the species-level trait value at the climate centre, exported to
`outputs/traits/<trait>_climate_response.csv.gz` (with a `_meta.csv` dictionary)
by the per-trait targets.

### The fitted model

`build_model_formula()` assembles the model from the climate-variable stems, so
the explicit form isn't visible in the notebook. With the two default climate
variables it is the following within-group-centred ("Mundlak") mixed model, in
`glmmTMB` syntax:

```r
log_value ~ log_annual_precipitation_mn + average_temperature_mn   # between-species
          + log_annual_precipitation_c  + average_temperature_c    # within-species
          + (1 | taxon_name)                                       # species intercept
          + (0 + log_annual_precipitation_c | taxon_name)          # species precip slope
          + (0 + average_temperature_c | taxon_name)               # species temp slope
```

- For each climate variable, `_mn` is the species' medoid (its climate centre)
  and `_c = obs − medoid` is the within-species deviation.
- The `_mn` terms capture **between-species** turnover across the continent; the
  `_c` terms capture the **within-species** response across a species' range.
- Random effects are an uncorrelated species intercept plus per-variable species
  slopes — no climate interaction and no intercept–slope correlation, matching
  the convergence-driven choices in the height analysis.
- The species-level value at the climate centre (where `_c = 0`) is the intercept
  plus the species random intercept.
- The `brms` backend fits the same formula with weakly informative priors.

The exact formula used for the fit (echoed live so it can't drift from the code):

```{r print-formula}
build_model_formula()
```

### Full posterior (BRMS backend, opt-in)

For the deliverable we refit with the BRMS backend. TMB gives a fast maximum-
likelihood point estimate, and for the *central* species means the two backends
agree closely (data dominate the weakly informative priors). What changes is the
**uncertainty**, and that is the deliverable's main product. TMB reports
species means conditional on plug-in point estimates of the variance components,
with asymptotic (delta-method) standard errors; the posterior instead gives the
full joint distribution of every quantity we report. Concretely:

- **Variance-component uncertainty is propagated.** TMB fixes the random-effect
  SDs at their ML values when forming species intervals; the posterior integrates
  over uncertainty in *how much* each species is shrunk toward the mean. This
  matters most for species with few records, where the shrinkage is itself poorly
  determined — exactly the species whose intervals we most need to trust.
- **The species mean is a derived, back-transformed quantity.** Each reported
  value is `intercept + species random intercept`, fitted on the log scale and
  exponentiated. Its posterior is correlated across parameters and asymmetric on
  the natural scale; a point estimate ± SE cannot represent that skew, whereas the
  posterior carries it through exactly.
- **Boundary/singular fits are regularised.** ML variance estimates can collapse
  to zero (degenerate partial pooling); the weakly informative priors on the SDs
  keep them off the boundary, giving sensible shrinkage for sparse traits.
- **It is the basis for full inference downstream** — calibrated credible
  intervals, the within/between decomposition *with* uncertainty, and (round 2)
  treating missing covariates / gap-filling as parameters to be imputed rather
  than dropped.

The BRMS backend is **opt-in**: set `run_brms <- TRUE` in `_targets.R` to add the
`brms_fits` / `brms_diag` targets. Each fit uses 4 chains with within-chain
threading (`reduce_sum`) and is cached on disk under `data-processed/brms_fits/`
(reused unless the model/data change). Always inspect the diagnostics: larger
traits need more iterations (e.g. `leaf_area` did not converge at `iter = 1500`).
One-time `cmdstanr::rebuild_cmdstan()` resolves stale precompiled-header warnings
when threading first turns on.

**Height is excluded from the BRMS backend and kept on TMB.** After unifying the
sources it carries ~306k records across ~10,200 species, i.e. ~30,000 random-
effect parameters — a NUTS fit there runs many hours (the per-iteration cost is
flat across warmup, so the mass-matrix adaptation never rescues it) with real risk
of memory pressure and divergences. The full posterior is not worth that for one
trait; TMB's asymptotic (delta-method) intervals are the pragmatic choice for
height. So the BRMS run fits every trait *except* height (`brms_traits` target).

### Fitted fixed effects by trait

Between-species (`_mn`) and within-species (`_c`) slopes for precipitation and
temperature, plus the global intercept, for each trait.

```{r summary-table}
trait_summary |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Across-species turnover

For each trait, the predicted species mean at the climate centre against the
centre's mean annual precipitation (log–log), with the across-species trend.
(The same figures are also written PNG + PDF to `outputs/traits/figures/` by the
`tmb_fig_*` targets.)

```{r centre-figures, results = "asis"}
for (tr in names(tmb_fits)) {
  cat("\n\n### ", tr, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(plot_trait_centres(tmb_fits[[tr]]$centres, tr, x = "precip", log_y = TRUE))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

## Round 2: simple means + combined product

The climate-centre model (round 1) covers species with enough records *and* a
climate medoid. For the remainder — low-coverage species, and species dropped for
having no medoid — we fall back to a simple per-species mean (the geometric mean
of all available records, since traits are log-normal). These run on the full,
un-medoid-filtered record pool, so every species with any data gets an estimate.

The combined product (`combined` target → `species_trait_means_combined.csv.gz`)
gives one **best estimate** per species × trait: the climate-centre estimate where
available, otherwise the simple mean, with a `method` flag recording which was
used.

### Coverage by method

How many species per trait are estimated by the climate-centre model vs the
simple-mean fallback.

```{r coverage}
combined |>
  count(trait_name, method) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(total = climate_centre + simple_mean) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Exported files

Per trait, in `outputs/traits/`:

- `<trait>_climate_response.csv.gz` — round-1 climate-centre estimates: one row
  per species with the predicted trait value at the climate centre (with
  interval), the centre climate, sample size, and species random effects.
- `<trait>_climate_response_meta.csv` — a column dictionary.
- `trait_model_summary.csv` — fitted fixed effects for every trait
  (`trait_summary_file` target).
- `species_trait_means_combined.csv.gz` — the integrated best-estimate product
  across all traits: climate-centre estimate where available, else the simple
  mean, with a `method` flag (`combined_file` target).
